stem: A 25-year-old patient presents with chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and abdominal pain. Inflammatory bowel disease is suspected. What is the gold standard for diagnosis?
expl: Colonoscopy (with ileoscopy) and multiple biopsies is the gold standard — it shows the pattern (continuous vs skip), gives histology and excludes infection/cancer.

why.A: CT shows complications, not the diagnosis.

stem: A 40-year-old man with Crohn’s disease underwent a 40 cm small bowel resection 2 years ago. He now presents with chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and signs of malnutrition. What is the most likely cause?
expl: Keyed short bowel syndrome — diarrhoea, weight loss and malnutrition after small-bowel resection. (Strictly, 40 cm is a modest resection — SBS usually needs < 200 cm remaining; terminal ileal loss can also cause bile-acid diarrhoea and B12 deficiency.)

why.C: Adhesive obstruction causes colic and vomiting.
why.D: Bacterial overgrowth is possible (strictures), but the key is SBS.

stem: A 35-year-old man with a history of Crohn’s disease underwent a small bowel resection 5 years ago. He now presents with two strictures each <3 cm, separated by 10 cm of normal bowel. What is the most appropriate management?

opts.t: Small bowel resection of the affected segment
Endoscopic balloon dilation of both strictures

expl: Recurrent Crohn's with previous resection and two short strictures separated by healthy bowel → stricturoplasty for both (preserves length, avoids short bowel).

why.B: Resecting a long segment wastes 10 cm of healthy bowel.
why.C: Balloon dilatation suits short accessible (anastomotic/colonic) strictures.
why.D: Stricturotomy isn't the standard surgical term here.

stem: Transmural inflammation with skip lesions and a cobblestone appearance — what is the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: Crohn's disease Short recall: the source supplies an answer without answer options.
ansText: Crohn's disease — transmural, skip lesions, cobblestone mucosa (deep linear ulcers between oedematous mucosa), granulomas.

stem: A male with long-standing ulcerative colitis (>10 years) is diagnosed with adenocarcinoma in the sigmoid colon. What is the best surgical option?
expl: Cancer in long-standing UC → the whole colon and rectum are at risk (field change, synchronous lesions) → (restorative) proctocolectomy.

stem: A patient with IBD (probably UC) has a severe flare with 10 bowel movements a day needing transfusion; CT shows colitis without perforation, and after 72 hours there is no improvement. What is the best surgical management?
ansText: Subtotal (total abdominal) colectomy with end ileostomy, leaving the rectal stump — failure of 48–72 h of intensive medical therapy in acute severe colitis; the rectum is not touched in the emergency.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with IBD (mild colitis on colonoscopy a year ago) presents with haematochezia. What is the cause?
ansText: A flare of her inflammatory bowel disease (the recall gave Crohn's flare); colorectal cancer must also be considered in long-standing colitis.

stem: A 32 year old male with vague abdominal pain, low grade fever and diarrhea is treated with antibiotics without significant improvement. Several weeks after the onset of symptoms he develops a skin lesion in his right lower abdominal quadrant that turns out to be an enterocutaneous fistula. The patient most likely suffers from which of the following?
expl: Weeks of pain, fever and diarrhoea not responding to antibiotics, then an enterocutaneous fistula → transmural disease = Crohn's.

why.C: Appendicitis is acute, and fistulas are rare.
why.D: UC is mucosal — fistulas are rare.

stem: 28-year-old women known to have Crohn’s disease Presented to ED with a history of 8-12 episodes of diarrhea/ day over the last 5 days. The electrocardiogram showed flattened T- waves. Which of the following is the most likely electrolyte abnormality?
expl: Severe diarrhea loses K⁺; flattened T waves = hypokalemia.

why.B: Can coexist; flat T waves point to K⁺.

stem: A case of a chron’s patient who underwent hemicolectomy as a management for his symptoms. However, he presented a few days later post-op complaining of signs and symptoms of local peritonitis. What’s the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms ?
expl: Local peritonitis a few days after a bowel resection with anastomosis → anastomotic leak until proven otherwise.

why.B: Causes recurrence later, not acute peritonitis.

stem: A 35 y/o female presented with progressive distention of the abdomen, and recently vomited twice. Examination showed Anal abcess. CT scan demonstrated edema in the terminal ileum. Which of the following is the best next step?
srcNote: (IBD) Incomplete choice set: options C and D are missing in the source.
expl: Keyed: active terminal-ileal Crohn's (oedema on CT, perianal abscess) with obstructive symptoms from inflammation → IV steroids to settle the inflammatory flare (after draining the abscess). 5-ASA enemas treat distal UC.

why.B: Topical 5-ASA doesn't reach the terminal ileum and is for UC.

stem: A 55 years old male known case of crohn's diease 10 years ago. Diagnosed with complex fistula and 4-cm perianal abcese. What is the best managment option :
expl: Complex fistula + abscess in Crohn's → incision and drainage + loose (draining) seton; then medical therapy (anti-TNF). Fistulotomy of a complex Crohn's fistula risks incontinence and non-healing.

why.B: Fistulotomy is only for simple low fistulas.
why.C: Sitz baths don't drain an abscess.

stem: which of the following is an indication for immediate exploratory laparotomy in patient with crohn disease?
expl: Free perforation (generalized peritonitis) is an emergency → immediate laparotomy. Fistulas and obstruction are usually managed first medically/electively.

why.B: Obstruction is first managed conservatively (most common indication, but not immediate).

stem: A 37 year old man with a 10 year history of ulcerative colitis who has been found to have a sessile polyp 10 cm from the anal verge with high-grade dysplasia Which one of the following is the most appropriate surgical procedure?
expl: High-grade dysplasia in long-standing UC → the whole colorectal mucosa is at risk → restorative total proctocolectomy with ileal J-pouch (removes all diseased mucosa, preserves continence).

why.B: Local excision leaves the field at risk.

stem: twenty-something y/o male with mild clinical signs of Crohn's colitis, what is the primary management?
expl: Mild Crohn's colitis → medical therapy (5-ASA/budesonide, immunomodulators/biologics); surgery only for complications or failure.

stem: Pt diagnosed with Crohn's 1 week ago, presented with intersphinteric-ano fistula, what is the best management option?
expl: Keyed infliximab — Crohn's perianal fistulas respond to anti-TNF therapy (with seton drainage if there is sepsis). Fistulotomy is avoided in Crohn's (poor healing, incontinence) except for simple low fistulas.

why.C: Cutting setons cause incontinence in Crohn's.
why.D: Too vague; medical therapy comes first.

stem: can't remember the question but it had something to do with crohn’s (pt needed to have small bowel resection due to distal small bowel lesion)

opts.t: Side by side primary bowel anastomosis
Wait for the frozen section and see if the margins are clear

srcNote: (Gallstone related disorders) Incomplete recall: the full stem is missing. The source key is reproduced but cannot be resolved from the recalled question.
expl: The full stem is missing. The source keyed cholecystectomy (filed under gallstone disorders) — that only fits a question about gallstones: terminal-ileal Crohn's or resection causes bile-salt loss → cholesterol gallstones. If the question asked how to restore continuity after a distal small-bowel resection, the answer would be primary (side-to-side) anastomosis; frozen sections aren't needed because ~2 cm grossly healthy margins are enough.

why.A: Correct (source key, for a gallstone-related stem).
why.B: The right choice for an elective Crohn's resection without sepsis.
why.C: Microscopic margins don't matter in Crohn's.
why.D: A stoma is for abscess, sepsis or high-dose steroids.

stem: A 36-year-old male presented with signs and symptoms of subacute bowel obstruction. Subsequent investigations showed that he has Cohn's disease of the small bowel with two short strictures confined to the terminal ileum. What is the best surgical management of his Crohn's strictures?
expl: Keyed resection: short strictures confined to the terminal ileum (the commonest Crohn's site) are best treated by ileocaecal resection; stricturoplasty suits multiple jejunoileal strictures or patients at risk of short bowel.

why.B: Stricturoplasty is reasonable, but the key prefers resection for localized terminal-ileal disease.
why.D: Bypass is abandoned (blind loop, cancer risk).

stem: A 30 year old woman presented to the emergency department with 6 bloody bowel movements per day. Blood pressure was 110/65 pulse, 110 per minute and temperature 38.5 C. Abdominal examination revealed diffuse tenderness all over the abdomen with guarding. WBC was 19x109 /L. Which one of the following is the appropriate next step in the management of this patient?

opts.t: High dose of intravenous steroids with observation.

expl: Severe colitis (6 bloody stools, fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis) with diffuse tenderness and guarding = peritonitis/perforation risk → emergency total colectomy with end ileostomy (rectum left).

why.A: Steroids are for severe colitis without peritonism.

stem: patient with crohn’s disease comes to the emergency department with obstruction he was taken to the OR for exploratory laparotomy it was found that he has 3 strictures and the proximal stricture was the cause of the obstruction What is the next step in management?

opts.t: Removal of the colon along with stricture.

srcNote: . strictureplasty ? (IBD) The source key includes a question mark and labels option A as strictureplasty; the original choice wording and uncertain key are preserved.
expl: Keyed "multiple stricture removal" — all significant strictures are dealt with at the same operation (usually by stricturoplasty, sometimes short resection) to avoid further obstruction and re-operation, while preserving bowel length.

why.B: Leaving the other strictures risks another obstruction.

stem: Which of the following is the most common indication for surgery in a patient who is diagnosed with Crohn’s disease?
srcNote: (IBD) - all of them are correct and mentioned in the same part in surgical davidson’s 7th edition page 258
expl: Intestinal obstruction (stricturing disease) is the commonest indication for surgery in Crohn's; perforation, bleeding and growth failure are also indications but less common.

stem: Which of the following represents a contraindication for strictureplasty in patients with Crohn’s disease at the time of surgery?

opts.t: A fistula at the level of the stricture
A stricture proximal to severe ileocecal disease

srcNote: ( IBD) Shwarts: Strictroplasty is contraindicated in pt with Intra-abdominal abscesses and intestinal fistulas.
expl: Stricturoplasty is contraindicated with a fistula, phlegmon or abscess at the site (and suspected cancer); multiple strictures are the main indication.

why.B: Long strictures can be done (Michelassi side-to-side).

stem: A male patient presented with recurrent fistula, bloody mucus stool and tenesmus, colonoscopy showed unhealthy rectum, what is the likely diagnosis?
srcNote: , both answers counted as correct. (IBD) The source accepts both answers. Other recalls give ulcerative colitis alone; these original differences are retained. Other source key (Final 429 A Q30 (p. 282)): Answer: D (IBD). In that version: D. Ulcerative colitis. Other source key (Final 428 Q17 (p. 303)): Answer: A. In that version: A. Ulcerative colitis.
expl: The source accepted both: recurrent fistulae and an unhealthy rectum suggest Crohn's (fistulizing perianal disease), while bloody mucus and tenesmus with rectal involvement suggest UC.

why.C: IBS doesn't cause fistulae or bleeding.

stem: Which one of the following is a proven risk factor for colon cancer?
expl: Long-standing UC is a proven risk factor (risk rises after 8–10 years, especially pancolitis). Red meat is associated, but UC is the clearly proven one in the key.

why.C: Red meat is associated, but the key chose UC.

stem: A 38 year old man who is known to have ulcerative colitis for 8 years on infliximab and imuran presented to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain and fever. On examination , he was found to have peritonitis. Chest X ray showed free air under diaphragm. He underwent exploratory laparotomy and was found to have sigmoid perforation. Which one of the following would be the optimal surgical procedure?

opts.t: Peritoneal lavage and creation of ileostomy.
Proctocolectomy with creation of ileal pouch.

expl: Perforated UC (free air, peritonitis) on immunosuppression → emergency total (subtotal) colectomy with end ileostomy; no restorative pouch in an emergency.

why.A: Lavage + ileostomy leaves the perforated colon.
why.D: A pouch isn't made in an emergency.

stem: Regarding crohn's disease:
expl: Keyed: Crohn's "usually has no malignant transformation" — cancer risk exists (Crohn's colitis) but is lower than UC. The rectum is usually spared, perianal disease is common, and inflammation is transmural.
